CUSTOMS ACT AMENDMENT The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 11, to amend the Customs Act-Mr. Usley-Mr. Johnston (Lake Centre) in the chair.
On section 5 (now section 3)-Cost plus reasonable profit.

When the committee rose I had begun to make one or two observations in reference to section 5, which is the new section 36 having to do with cost plus reasonable profit. I was asked, by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I believe, this question: Is the hon. member suggesting that these new machines which he calls obsolete-my words were, "obsolete to a certain extent"- should be permitted to come in at a price lower than the cost of manufacture? I believe I replied to that, "yes"; but I did not mean: Yes, lower than cost of manufacture. What I meant was: Lower than this section would call for. What I had in mind was that the following words are struck out of the section as it stood and do not appear in the new section:
...and the minister shall be the sole judge of what shall constitute a reasonable advance m the circumstances and his decision thereon shall be final.
These words, which have been deleted from the new section, constituted in my opinion a protection inasmuch as, on the one hand, they prevented this market from being flooded with cheap material and, on the other, did not prevent the importation at a reasonable price of machinery that would not be made in this country because of the small demand for it. The section as it stood would not prevent the importation of such machinery at a price which the minister would determine as representing a reasonable amount of profit over cost. In connection with the prevention of imports into Canada of material made in very large quantities, principally in the United States, at prices with which Canadian manufacturers cannot compete, I felt that the words that had been struck out afforded a certain amount of protection to Canadian employment. All I have in mind in the remarks I am making is the safeguarding as far as possible of employment in industry in Canada. Last week in Toronto I came across a circumstance which, I think, will illustrate my point. I am referring now to a well known line of faucets or taps or bibs used by plumbers and steamfitters, a fairly high class line which is made in this country and was sold to the trade at approximately S7.50 a pair. I am informed that similar lines are now brought into Canada and sold
Customs Act

here at $4 a pair. The Canadian employees of a company manufacturing a similar line of taps, faucets and bibs will be up against a loss of employment to the extent of such importations. Under the old section the minister was the sole judge of what constituted a reasonable advance, and his decision thereon was final. The minister had the power to prevent the dumping on the Canadian market of such material, whereas under the new section I do not see where employment is safeguarded to the same extent. Perhaps I have not interpreted the seotion properly, but I cannot see where under it the same protection is given to employment that was afforded under the old section. Perhaps the minister can enlighten me in that regard.

This amendment does not make any difference at all in principle in the section that heretofore existed. Section 36, as it has existed up to the present, provided that the value for duty should not be less than the cost of production plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit, and the only criticism was as to the method of administration of that section. The criticism of importers in Canada and exporters in the United States was that an advance was being added that was unreasonable, and that it was being added for the purpose of giving more protection to manufacturers in this country than the section itself contemplated. The only change that is being made is the provision that hereafter such advance is not to be greater than that which in the ordinary course of business, under normal conditions of trade, is added, in the case of similar goods to those under consideration, by manufacturers or producers of goods of the same class or kind in the country of export. There is a point as to the discretion of the minister being removed by the proposed amendment. The intention is that in case of a dispute as to whether a proper advance is being added to the cost of production in the country of origin, there should be a resort to the tariff board instead of to the minister, just as is done under section 43. I should like to point out that sections 36 and 43 are comparatively new sections which apply to a very small proportion of the importations into this country.
To meet specifically the points he has raised my hon. friend has approached the problem from two opposite starting points. In the first place he has suggested that the values for duty fixed for machinery which, though new or unused, is obsolete or nearly so, in future must be too high with that section in the Customs Act. That was the point my hon. friend was making before six o'clock.

Perhaps there may be some difficulty there in theory, but only in theory. The hon. gentleman will realize that if the machinery is not machinery of a class or kind made or produced in Canada that special duty, the dumping duty as it is popularly called, does not apply at all, so that any fear of dumping duty is out of the way and the problem is confined to the ad valorem rate which, in the case put, he fears might be reckoned on too high a value.
I have in mind item 427 of the tariff, which affords a protection of about 27i per cent.

But what would happen in practice would be this:	In all probability
we would take the invoice value. There would be no occasion for an investigation as to cost of production in the case put by the hon. member; as a matter of practice such an investigation would never take place. These investigations into cost of production take place, as a matter of practice, on the complaint of manufacturers in this country, who say that they are being subjected to unfair competition. If they do say that, we have to put in motion the machinery of investigation in the country of origin, and our investigators try to arrive at the cost of production there. But in the case put by my hon. friend his fears are purely fanciful, if I may express it in that way. It would never work out as he suggests.
Now, with regard to the point raised by my hon. friend just now, namely his fear that, with the ministerial discretion removed, the values may be fixed too low, I am unable to follow his reasoning. The minister is just as likely to fix the values too 'high as too low, and it is a question as to who is to fix them, whether the final court should be the minister or the tariff board. We think that for the comparatively rare cases that will arise under this seotion there is no objection to the tariff board having the final say instead of the minister.

I hardly expected this
bill to get to committee to-day, and I have not under my hand certain material that I wished to bring to the attention of the minister and of the committee when dealing with this section. The point I wish to raise- and it is something that has been in my mind for a good many years-is that in the administration of customs affairs in Canada there has grown up a practice-I am going to put it rather crudely and sharply in order to bring out the point at once-of tariffs

Customs Act
being made by officials of the department. I will demonstrate to the minister what I mean, and I trust that in putting it in that way it will not be considered that I am attacking the officials of the department or the department as such, because I think it is a practice which has grown up over a great many years.
_ The committee will notice that by section 5 of the bill, which refers to section 36 of the Customs Act, part of section 36 is deleted. The minister read that section a moment ago, but I will read it again and perhaps indicate to the hon. member for Davenport another point of interest in connection with it. The operative part of this section has been retained; the part that has been dropped, for which another part has been substituted, is the qualifying part. In the part that remains we read the following:
The value for duty of new or unused goods shall m no case be less than the actual cost ot production of similar goods at date of shipment direct to Canada plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit ...
For the purpose of my argument I want to stop there and, by the way, in order to make clear something I shall say later on, the part that has been deleted, referring to the ministers control in the past, operated only when appeal was made to the minister. In other words the operative part of this section was administered by officials through departmental bulletins, not under the sanction of an order in council, not under sanction of the statutes, but as a part of the ordinary administration or administrative action of the officials. The reason I said a moment ago that I am sorry the subject is up now is that I had a short time ago a bulletin, I have forgotten the number, but if I remember rightly it was 4035, issued in 1933. I sent it away to get verification of prices of certain articles mentioned; therefore I do not have it here to present to the committee. This bulletin refers to certain classes of goods, certain types of rubber treated cloth, imitation leather; there is a technical term for it-some hon. member in the furniture trade may know what I refer to-pyroxylin I think it is. It describes a certain type of treated cloth which may be used as imitation leather. I think, for instance, railway car blinds are made of it. I cannot put my finger on the item without having the documents before me, but there is in the tariff an omnibus item in which several years ago a number of different kinds of commodities were included; part of the item is clothing, part is rubber treated cloth and part is this imitation leather, and so on. To my mind it should not be so included, but there it is. Now the department issued this
bulletin in 1933 fixing value for duty on about thirty or forty descriptions of this class of material, dividing them into certain classes and then subdividing them again by weight, and in this bulletin they fixed a value for duty, without any sanction by order in council but as an ordinary matter of administrative action. For this particular item a value of sixty cents was fixed. I am informed on good authority-and it was to verify that that I sent away for certain information-that this article can be purchased in the United States for twelve cents. There is only one manufacturer of it in Canada, that is Canadian Industries, a subsidiary of British Chemicals and of Duponts. That is British Chemicals, Canadian Industries and Duponts are all more or less interlocked, and there is pretty much of a cartel and division of territory.
I have now had a copy of this bulletin handed to me by some kind friend. It is bulletin No. 4035, and the tariff item is No. 532. The spelling of the word in this bulletin is wrong, it is "proxylin," but the correct spelling is, I believe, "pyroxylin." The official title of the bulletin is appraisers' bulletin No. 4035; the indexed subject is rubber-coated fabrics and pyroxylin coated fabrics and papers from the United States; it is signed by Robert Breadner, for the guidance of customs and excise officers, and refers to file No. 176210 and current values for duty. It then goes on to say:
From the information before the department, rubber-coated fabrics and pyroxylin coated fabrics and papers imported from the United States may be appraised under section 36 (2) of the Customs Act, in accordance with the following net prices-
Then there is a long list of prices; I am taking one on the back page:
Sheetings (bookbinding and novelties) five to eight ounces, sixty cents a pound.
That is an instruction to all collectors of customs that they must value this article coming into Canada at that price. I am told that this material is manufactured in Canada by Canadian Industries, and in the United States by Dupont. I am told also that it can be bought in the United States from the manufacturers for twelve cents and up. I am told that it can be landed in Canada duty paid, apart from this special valuation for duty, with the excess special charge and the poundage charge which amount to sixty-eight per cent, at these excessively high rates- sixty-eight per cent is pretty high-at around fifty cents. Nevertheless the bulletin says that it shall be valued at sixty cents at the point of shipment in the United States, which is of course absolutely wrong.
Customs Act

Now I come to the other point that I have already mentioned. While it is manufactured in Canada solely by Canadian Industries, it is manufactured in the United States by Duponts, the parent, or brother or sister company of Canadian Industries, but it is also manufactured over there by four or five other companies, so that there is competition in the buying market, but there is no competition in the selling market. Now, if the appraisers of the government fixed this price of sixty cents as a fair value by reference to Duponts in the United States, unquestionably the Dupont people would fix the value at a point which would suit the purposes of the affiliated company here. I do not think there is any question about that. But had a search been made of the different manufacturers in the United States I am satisfied that the department would have found an entirely different story.
That is only one illustration. I have not had time to check a number of others but I understand there are others in this bulletin, perhaps not quite as striking but more or less of the same kind. The minister will know what I am particularly labouring here, that apart altogether from the qualification in this clause, whether it is the new one or the old one, bulletins of this kind were sent out, I understand, quite frequently and as a matter of course. Now I stand subject to correction, but I shall have to be definitely shown that I am wrong-
You are right.

I think I am right. So far as I could see this bulletin had no sanction in an order in council or in any statute, except an assumed power under section 36 by the appraisers' division. What I want to suggest to the government is-and I wish the Prime Minister were in his seat, because this is a practical application of the doctrine he has frequently enunciated-that parliament shall not delegate its power recklessly. Certainly no official, no department or no branch of a department should be permitted to fix values for duty by issuing a bulletin, without a definite sanction by law and through an order in council.
The Prime Minister has frequently criticized the fixing of tariff rates by order in council, and in a measure I share his view, except to the extent that conditions may arise when it is necessary to take prompt action in order to stabilize a market. Such conditions would arise in connection with fruits and vegetables in the spring of the year, and under such circumstances fixation by order in

council may be justified. But certainly in connection with manufactured articles of this kind, among which are trench cloth, quarter lining, raincoat material, hospital sheeting, which no doubt is a rubber sheeting, combined sport fabrics, sheeting, drills, sateens, moleskins, sock linings and so on, values should not be fixed by bulletin.
May I say that I do not believe that condition is remedied by the amendment. I imagine that with the attention of the government drawn to the condition instructions will probably be issued to the effect that no more bulletins of the kind shall be sent out without sanction or authority by order in council. That would be the natural action. But as a matter of fact I understand this bulletin is now in force, and I was startled when I received that information. I had known of extreme powers being exercised, and particularly a few years ago when the late Mr. Breadner wras in charge, although I do not like to reflect upon a man who is no longer here. However, he had certain stem views. Under such circumstances too much is left to the decision or the whim of an official when he is left with authority to issue a bulletin of this kind. I believe the minister should have a careful examination made of all outstanding bulletins, of which I believe there are hundreds. I am speaking without a great deal of detailed knowledge, but I do suggest that an examination be made and the practice of fixing duties in that way should be abandoned.
Before leaving the subject we have been discussing may I direct the attention of the minister to item 532 of the tariff which covers the class of goods to which I have been referring. In that item we shall see how we have brought into one item a mass of unrelated articles such as clothing, wearing apparel and articles, made from woven fabrics, and all manufactures, wholly or partially completed composed wholly of cotton n.o.p.; fabrics wholly of cotton, coated or impregnated, n.o.p., 25 per cent, 30 per cent and 35 per cent, plus a special duty per pound of two cents, three and a half cents and four cents.'
A few days ago I saw a number of samples of what is known as impregnated or coated cloth coming under this item, and I learned that a great variety of manufactured products come under it. It is associated with clothing, wearing apparel, articles made from woven fabrics and so on, so that a great many items come under it. To give a power such as that exercised in the bulletin to which I have referred is in my opinion all wrong.

Customs Act
My point in rising is to direct the minister's attention to the fact that while the amendment does limit the advance that can be placed upon valuation it does not remove what hitherto has given authority for the issue of these bulletins. I should like the minister to take special note of that fact, because I believe it is a purely administrative matter rather than one calling for an amendment. The section states:
Such advance not to be greater than that which in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade, is added, in the case of goods similar to the particular goods under consideration, by manufacturers or producers of goods of the same class or kind in the country of export.
That simply means that they are permitted to add a fair profit and handling charges to the costs of production, and I can see no great objection to the provision. Nor do I believe anything is lost-and I do not make this observation in disrespect of this or any other minister-by the repeal of the former wording, namely:
-and the minister shall be the sole judge of what shall constitute a reasonable advance in the circumstances and his decision thereon shall be final.
As I understand it, the practice has been that the minister's decision in these matters was given only when there was an appeal to him against the normal activities and practices of the department. In that respect I should like to say-and I might as well say it now, while this clause is under discussion-that we have set up a tariff board to perform certain functions. Under the present chairman I believe the tariff board has proven to be an effective body. I believe it is a body which is winning public confidence, and such a body must have time to establish its record, its practices, its methods and its decisions before it is able to win public confidence. I do believe the present tariff board is doing that and I believe further that as an institution it is sound. Undoubtedly, however, the Minister of Finance has received great numbers of applications in connection with the present tariff. He will correct me if I exaggerate when I state that possibly he has received thousands of applications.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct.

Obviously no Minister of Finance could cope with such a situation. I understand that he and those who have preceded him in office, in the few months preceding the presentation of a budget are literally swamped with delegations and with demands with which it is not humanly possible to deal. Nor could the minister's officers deal with
them, because the time they should be spending in studying the items and their merits is spent in receiving delegations. I venture to say that at this time the minister is almost at his wits' end to know how to deal with the applications made to him concerning the tariff. For these reasons while we are amending the act I believe we should extend to the tariff board the reference of matters pertaining to the revision of the tariff or changing rates of duty, customs and so on. My suggestion is that in that respect we should enlarge the powers and duties of the tariff board. I venture to say that if when this house sits as a committee of ways and means the Minister of Finance could come before it and say that the item had been studied by the tariff board, and that the board had made certain findings, such item would pass with very little question, unless a matter of policy with respect to general tariff duties was involved. On the other hand, if the minister is not fortified in that way, there will be more critical examination of the items that are presented to the house. So it will be far better if the annual revision of the tariff such as we have from time to time should be the product of the tariff board, and therefore I entirely agree with the minister in his observation of a moment ago that when there is any question under this particular section it should be settled by way of appeal to the tariff board. I think it is quite the proper thing to drop this final and unalterable decision of the minister in accordance with the act as it previously stood.

I thank the member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) for bringing the case of pyroxylin to my attention. There is no question in my mind that there are cases such as that where the values were fixed some years ago. From the terms of the bulletin which he has read to the committee I should think the values must have been fixed at least three or four years ago.
It is dated Ottawa, April 22, 1933.

Yes. Undoubtedly it is desirable that the values fixed under section 36 should be reviewed as fast as we can deal with them. A great many of them have been reviewed and a number of them have been changed. The section is not so very much different from the one that was in existence at that time. Undoubtedly the officials of the department will have to do the work of investigating and fixing these values, and if anyone brings any mistake to the attention of the department the matter will certainly be gone into and the values brought into line with the
Customs Act

facts. If the cost of production in the United States was from twelve to fifteen cents, and the value was fixed at sixty cents, that was illegal action on the part of the departmental official who did this. It is for that very reason, because there were such extravagant advances on the cost of production, that this amendment to the section has been introduced. As the section stood, the minister had unrestricted discretion to say what was a reasonable advance over selling cost and profit. Now we provide by law that such advance shall not be greater than that which in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade is added in the case of goods similar to the particular goods under consideration by manufacturers or producers of goods of the same class or kind in the country of export. This amendment is designed to meet the situation which the hon. member has placed before the committee. He is quite right in saying that a change in the law will not in itself be sufficient unless we actually go to work and apply it. All I can say is that it is certainly my purpose to try and get rid of all these extravagant valuations under section 36, just as we have got rid of most of them under section 43.
Since six o'clock I have given consideration to the criticism of the section that was voiced by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the leader of the opposition, that the section does not make it sufficiently clear that the advance in question is to be the advance added when sold for home consumption.
Domestic consumption as distinct from export.
It was the intention that that was the advance to be added, and therefore I am going to ask my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce to move an amendment to make it quite clear.
I move, Mr. Chairman, that section 5 as printed, now section 3, be amended by adding at the end thereof within the quotation marks the words "when sold for home consumption."
That covers it.
Amendment agreed to.

Can the minister inform
the committee whether or not there was under the United States customs or tariff laws a provision similar to that of our section 36 as it now stands?

I have no knowledge of
that, but so far as I am aware there is no such provision.

Might I assume, then,
that so far as this government is concerned there has certainly been no arrangement with the government of the United States that if there are such provisions in the United States laws suitable amendments will be introduced similar to those introduced here?

So far as I know there
have been no complaints whatsoever by Canadian exporters similar to those that were voiced by Canadian importers with regard to these provisions.

I am afraid my hon.
friend has not conferred with many Canadian exporters. I shall not take up tihe time of the committee to detail some of the difficulties they meet with in endeavouring to export to the United States, but in addition to the point raised by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, which has now been dealt with, there is in connection with this section something else which is giving me considerable concern, and that is the ambiguity of its language. I am sure the minister as a member of the bar is desirous that legislation should be clear and specific in its terms. I am much concerned as to what is the meaning of the words "in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade."
I think in order to make my point clear to the minister I must review very briefly something that was said this afternoon. The minister pointed out this afternoon that the general section of the Customs Act with respect to values was section 35, which starts off by saying "whenever any duty ad valorem is imposed on any goods imported into Canada," certain conditions shall prevail. Now that must apply to all goods imported. Section 36 says, "The value for duty of new or unused goods shall in no case be less than the actual cost of production," and so forth. The minister stated that this section did not apply generally but applied only in a limited number of cases, if I understood him correctly. I think with respect to that he must be in error; surely if the section means anything at all it means that despite the provision with respect to any goods contained in section 35 where the goods are new or used goods, the value shall not be less than the actual cost of production plus selling cost and profit. It seems to me that no matter what may have been the intention at the time of its enactment this section has, in large measure, in the administration of the department been used to deal with importations into this country by subsidiaries of American parent companies. That

Customs Act
has been the main purpose of the section according to my experience, and the difficulty arose that a parent company would export to a subsidiary in Canada goods at any prices they chose to fix as between themselves. It matters not to the parent company at what price the goods are sold because they own all the stock in the Canadian company. But that Canadian subsidiary may be in competition with other Canadian concerns, which may or may not be fully Canadian owned but which are not direct subsidiaries. The markup, as it was called in the vernacular of the department, was to produce a fair price when the parent company sold. I say that during the past four or five years, if not previously, that section has been used with respect to a large part of our imports. It must have been when we consider that, according to the statistics I had three months ago, there are in this country 1,800 subsidiaries of American companies.

Where a fair market value
has been established in the country of origin, this section would not be needed.
I am dealing with the invoice at which an exporter would export goods to the importer in Canada.

If that were less than the
fair market value in the country of origin the dumping duty would apply without the application of this section.

That is the very reason
why an importer in Canada desiring to import goods from a United States parent company came to the department and said, "I can buy my goods for this price in the United States, how much do you say I must mark them up to cover the items of selling cost and profit?" Under the old section someone in the department, subject to the approval of the minister, had definite power to fix that price. What happens now? This section now reads:
-such advance not to be greater than that which in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade, is added,
Am I to take prices during a period of depression as prices under normal conditions of trade? The (minister may say that that is not what the section means at all; that it means the normal conditions of trade in any particular group of industries dealing in that product in the country of export at the time of export. Well, then, I say to my hon. friend, if that is so-we will assume that there is an allegation that prices are being slaughtered for the time being in the country of origin because of competition in the trade-who is going to say what is the fair market value, plus the selling cost, plus profit? Who is
going to determine what should be the margin of profit? Who is going to determine whether there should be a one per cent return on the capital invested, a two per cent return, a three per cent return and so on? All this is left indefinite and ambiguous under this provision. Under the old section the minister had power to fix this; under this section, apparently the only person who has the power to fix it is a collector, an appraiser or sotoe departmental official.
The hon. member for Kootenay East complained a moment ago about the past administration of some of the officials. If there was trouble in the past when it was definite as to who had the ultimate power, surely under this ambiguous wording the problem is going to be confusion confounded. The minister may say that the collector or appraiser has the power to make the fixation and if someone disagrees with it they can go to the tariff board under subsection 4 of section 38. I think my hon. friend will agree that if we get down to the point where .the tariff board, an administrative body, not a representative of the government, not a minister of the crown, fixes what shall be the profit and what shall be the selling cost, we are creating the tariff board into a legislative body. The supreme court has determined already that they cannot be a legislative body. If that decision is good, we are left with a section under which there is no one who has the legal capacity to determine ultimately what shall be "in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade." I am not attempting to quarrel with the policy of the government; I disagree with it, as I made clear when speaking on the Canada-United States trade pact. I am dealing particularly with the proposed amendment, and I suggest to the minister that if these words should come before the courts for construction, they will have extreme difficulty in determining what this legislative body was endeavouring to say when it used the words, "in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade." I suggest to the minister that he should consider seriously getting a more specific definition as to what is intended.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Lawson) has made a valuable contribution to the debate, which contribution I appreciate. His argument has been to some extent legal and a little technical. Undoubtedly under the amendment proposed to the committee, the department in the first instance fixes the value for duty purposes under section 36. The hon. gentleman said that that would be done by a collector or an appraiser, but I
Customs Act

submit that it would really be the minister. Under section 2 of the act setting up the Department of National Revenue, known as the Department of National Revenue Act, the minister is given the management and direction of the department and is to hold office during pleasure. The difference between the old and new sections is that the minister's decision as to value is not necessarily final. The old section stated that the minister shall be the sole judge of what shall constitute a reasonable advance in the circumstances and his decision thereon shall be final. It is the intention of the government that instead of the minister's decision being final, as heretofore, the importer shall have the right to go to the tariff board on this point. It is possible that the tariff board has not jurisdiction under the existing sections, in view of the decision to which the hon. gentleman referred, but that is a matter which can be remedied very easily. Subsection 4 of section 11 of the Tariff Board Act reads:
The board shall have such powers and perform such duties under this part as are assigned to it by any act of the parliament of Canada or by the governor in council.
This act will confer jurisdiction under the provisions of the Tariff Board Act. That act says that the board shall have such jurisdiction as may be conferred upon it by any act of parliament.

I do not know whether I understand my right hon. friend's argument, but I say that if there is any difficulty as to jurisdiction, it can be remedied by an order in council under section 11 of the Tariff Board Act. Because of the reasons stated by the hon. member for Kootenay East, I submit that that is a very just arrangement. We told the United States negotiators that this would be the way we would apply this section from now on and there might be objections to inserting a provision that the minister's decision in the matter would be final in view of the well known fact that a great many of these values are now, or have been in the past, too high. We are trying to review them to bring them into line. If we agreed to put into the act a provision that they shall be reasonable, and immediately couple this with a provision such as was heretofore in the act, stating that the minister's decision would be final, it would appear as if we were not carrying out the spirit and intent of the agreement into which we entered with the United States. I do not see any objection in the world to leaving that matter in the hands of a competent board to decide, and the question of jurisdiction can be dealt with at any moment if the jurisdiction is defective. The other

point is involved, as to the meaning of the words "in the ordinary course of business under normal conditions of trade." As I understood the hon. gentleman, he said that in some transactions there is no ordinary course of business; there are no normal conditions, because the parent company is selling to its subsidiary and not selling to a similar body in the United States. That, I believe, is the basis of his argument.
It might be selling to other companies in the United States.

If it is, then there is an ordinary course of business; there are normal conditions of trade, and there is no difficulty whatsoever in applying the section. If there is an ordinary course of business; if there are normal conditions of trade, then you try by investigation to arrive at what the reasonable advance is under these conditions then you apply it and obtain the value for duty purposes. If however there is no ordinary course of business and no normal condition by reason of the uniqueness of the transaction, then you have to fall back on the word "reasonable" and apply a reasonable advance on the cost of production. I do not know why I should defend the section at such length. I see many objections to the section, and have in the past, but I think we should retain it for the time being at least to see how it works. I do not think, however, that the objections advanced by the hon. gentleman are unanswerable.

Let me put to my hon. friend a specific instance. A parent company in the United States is selling an article to a subsidiary in Canada at a unit price of ten cents. In the market at the place from which the article is exported directly to Canada the ordinary selling price under the conditions of trade then prevailing is ten cents. Now the conditions of trade then prevailing are these: Because there is in the country of export a production far in excess of demand there is tremendous competition and all concerns manufacturing that article and selling it dn the country of export at ten cents a unit get from it cost of production plus cost of selling, plus one-half of one per cent on the total capital invested. I ask my hon. friend this question: Under this section, is that a normal condition of trade, or is it the normal condition of trade that the price should be eleven cents a unit in the United States, let us say for example, so as to pay on the capital invested a return of three per cent? Which is it? Under these words "normal conditions of trade" I do not know,

I observe that the language used is exactly that used in the letters exchanged between the Minister of External Affairs, speaking through the Charge d'affaires, and the department at Washington:

We have merely enacted the terms of the letter and made it into a statute-there is no doubt about that-adding to it the words which have been added this evening as an amendment. In other words, the government's view is that it is essential to use the

I think the language is very good.

Knowing Mr. Wrong's capacity to use excellent English I should say there is no doubt about that. With respect to the general question, may I observe that there is nothing more fatal than to compare incomparable things. To compare prices in 1936 with prices in 1933 and to complain of the terms of values fixed by Mr. Breadner is a wholly improper thing to do. As a matter of fact Mr. Breadner in 1933 was acting under the instructions of his minister, who fixed the values, and in 1933 we were attacked in this country, as we had never been in our history, by goods from parent companies in the United States seeking markets here. In our endeavour to keep plants working in this country to supply Canadian requirements rather than to bring in goods from the United States, we had recourse to this section, as the hon. gentleman knows, and I think I heard him complain about it at the time. He thought we went too far, but as a matter of fact, rightly or wrongly, it was the only method by which we saw any opportunity of retaining in Canada work for those who supplied Canadian requirements in that class of goods. It is also well to remark that in some instances there has been a vast expansion of industrial activity on the part of those who supply certain types of goods that were covered by the bulletin of the appraisers in 1933. It is no longer limited to the United States; it is of general application, and what was originally a mere exchange of communications looking to a new procedure with respect to administration as between two countries has now in fact become part of the general law of the country, applying to importations from all countries, wherever there has been an application of the

principles of section 36. That, I think, is abundantly clear. I should like to support very strongly the argument presented by the bon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George by pointing out to the committee what actually happens in actual practice before the tariff board, as some members may not have appeared before the tariff board in hearings as I have. When application is made to the board they require a written submission, and the person making the application is virtually in the position of plaintiff. In the case we have in mind it must be borne in mind that as a pferequisite to the existence of the duty which is to be attacked -the government of this country has functioned and1 determined to its own satisfaction that there is an injurious effect on the interests of Canadian producers or manufacturers; being of that opinion it authorized its minister to do something, and he has functioned. Now, as pointed out by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, the tariff board makes copies of the applications as filed, with the reasons therefor, and it is under obligation to circularize and send them to every interest in Canada affected. It asks those interested for a return, in other words for a brief or a factum as against that which has been alleged by the plaintiff. It naturally takes time for this to be prepared, and when the tariff board has before it that which I shall call a factum, for want of a better term, it then determines whether or not there is a necessity for a public hearing. In this case it provides that there shall be a public hearing, but even though there is an obligatory provision for a public hearing, if the tariff board is to proceed intelligently with that public hearing it must have before it the allegations, or arguments, or facts. Generally speaking, subject to these necessary delays, the plaintiff has the conduct of the proceedings.
Let us assume that it is a private party making an application so that we shall not be making any allegation against any foreign government. By devious means at his command, that person can delay the hearing. All he has to do to succeed in his case is to prevent its being heard for a period of three months. In the first place, I say that three months is far too short a period for the involved questions which are bound to arise. In the second place, I say that a term which automatically benefits the plaintiff in the event of his own delay, which bonuses him for delay, should certainly not appear in this bill. If, in order to carry out the terms of the obligations contained in the letter to the Japanese government, this government- feels
Customs Act

that it must insert this most unusual provision in a statute, then I say that at least there ought to be some provision to make it incumbent upon the person who is going to attack or appeal from the duty as fixed by the minister to give some notice of his appeal.
To do it within a certain time.

To do it within a certain time; to serve his allegations, his notice of appeal; to do something to protect those Canadian producers and manufacturers who must prima facie be prejudicially or injuriously affected. I ask the minister as the representative of the government to consider seriously the implications in the last clause of this section which automatically sets aside that which the government and the minister have determined by the mere failure of the tariff board to function.

There are just two points to which I should like to direct attention. In the first place, I should like to say to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that this is not and cannot be an inquiry into the cost of production in the country of origin. There is no necessity for the government making any investigation as to the cost of production, say in Japan. That situation could not arise at all. The tariff board addresses itself to one question of fact only, whether the value fixed by the minister is necessary to prevent the importation of goods into Canada from prejudicially or injuriously affecting the interests of Canadian producers or manufacturers.
Surely the cost of production and the exchange rate must be factors in determining that?
The cost of Canadian product; ;n, not the cost of foreign production.
Of necessity, both must be factors.

I do not understand the
observations of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson). Where goods are coming m, it is the price at which they are quoted, not the cost a>t which they are produced, that concerns the Canadian manufacturer.

The price at which they are offered for sale.
Mr. ILSLE1 : That is what the Canadian manufacturer is concerned with, not with the cost at which they are produced. It is a matter which can be determined quite speedily; it does not require any investigation in a foreign country. That is the first point. With regard

to the point brought out by the hon. member for South York, that the time is not sufficient, I think we must assume that a court such as the tariff board will act with some sense of responsibility and regard for propriety. The idea that they would permit an importer to prevent them from making the declaration until three months had gone by is something beyond the realm of possibility.
That is exactly what you are providing for.

The provision of the three months' term is to impose an obligation upon the tariff board to act promptly so that the interested parties may not be tied up for an indefinite period and the government be subject to the accusation that they had put something in there that was not workable.

I suggest to the minister
that if this section goes into effect there will be times when a sufficient number of appeals of this character will be before the board to make it impossible for that board to function with respect to all of them.
There are not going to be many appeals because there are not going to be many fixed values.

If that takes place; if there is a delay beyond the three months and the valuation lapses, it will be a simple matter for the department to make another valuation which will be good for at least another three months.

I do not see why not.

That could not be done
and good faith still be preserved with the foreign country.

There is still the difficulty to which the hon. member for York South made some slight reference. The application should be made within a certain period of time, and this matter divides itself into two branches: First, the public revenue and, second, the conduct of business. For instance, if duties are paid on a rate which is subsequently found to be improper, it is obvious that refunds must be made and the question of revenue is affected. That is one side of the matter. The other side is the question of the convenience of the people concerned. In all our provisions about appeals from summary convictions we provide that the appeal must be made within fourteen days of the date of conviction or that certiorari must be taken within so many weeks or days. We

Customs Act
are fixing a period of time after which the appeal is discharged. The minister says that he has made up his mind that he will not make many fixed valuations, but in these uncertain economic conditions he cannot tell when he may be almost driven to do this. We sometimes have the habit of thinking that these things affect only one country when, in fact, they affect every countiy in the world.
As an illustration, let me mention Czechoslovakia. Our exports to that country have been practically nothing. The late government had under consideration whether or not the agreement with that country should be permitted to continue. We buy substantial quantities of goods from Czechoslovakia, but we ship practically nothing. If one takes the trouble to look inside the pair of gloves he is wearing to see where they are made, he will most likely find "made in Czechoslovakia." This applies to other countries on this continent, such as the United States. A substantial portion of a certain class of footwear is imported from Czechoslovakia. It will be remembered that the great Bata who met his death in an aeroplane accident, established a factory near London and created a great deal of difficulty. His old firm shipped substantial quantities of goods into this country. That, in my judgment, is one of the reasons why we should fix the time within which appeal should be taken.
Then there is the other side of the matter which I once more urge upon the minister. I wonder what any member of this committee would think if he were told that when a conviction had been made by a court, in the event of an appeal being taken, instead of the appeal lapsing by non-prosecution or by effiuxion of time, resulting in the original conviction standing, although a minister of the crown had exercised his discretion honestly and to the best of his ability, it is no longer his discretion that stands but the appeal, which becomes effective by effluxion of time. I venture to say that in all our statute laws in the British empire you will not find anything like it. I have read a great many of them from necessity-I do not say that I have read them all-and certainly, if you propounded that proposition in connection with an ordinary matter, one would think it unbelievable.
Let us take a case. The minister deals with an importation that comes from Czechoslovakia, an importation of rubber boots and shoes, tennis shoes, and he finds that the ad valorem duty is so insignificant, and his officials advise him, that it is desirable and necessary to place a fixed value upon these 12739-131
shoes. He does so; he places a fixed value which, for the sake of argument, we will say is fifty cents; that sounds very easy. The invoice price, as a matter of fact, was only twenty cents. The importer here at once takes an appeal to the tariff board. The tariff board is very busy; it does the best it can; it hears a part of the evidence and is unable to arrive at a conclusion; rushed with business it does not observe very closely what the time was, so that the three months go by from the date the appeal was taken, and on the day after the passing of the three months the twenty cents becomes the operative price at which these goods are to be valued for duty purposes. The minister had declared that Canadian industry was prejudicially affected because any value as low as twenty cents was unfair and prejudicial to Canadian manufacturers, and therefore he fixed a value of fifty cents. Now, instead of the result of the lapsing of the appeal being a valuation of fifty cents, the invoice price from Czechoslovakia of twenty cents will stand as the value. The minister has exercised honest discretion and yet he finds himself overruled in that way. I do not think you will find anything of that sort in the history of appeals. If, for instance, an appeal in the supreme court is not prosecuted it is dismissed for lack of prosecution; the appeal is dismissed automatically. In this case, by the mere effluxion of time, after the short period of three months, the appeal stands; it is not dismissed but allowed. The appeal is allowed and the original valuation of twenty cents stands.
I ask the minister in all seriousness to consider the point. I have done my duty as far as I see it in directing attention to the matter as clearly as I can, and I submit that he should not make a departure and establish in the statutes of the country a precedent which I at any rate have not heretofore seen. There may be cases

I do not say there are not, but I have not seen any-in which nonprosecution results in the allowing of an appeal. I think there should be an amendment in that sense.
I direct attention, only as a matter of form, to the desirability of having the language uniform throughout the section. In one case reference is made to the appeal and in another instance reference is made to the application. It might be well to refer to it in uniform terms. One of the rules which draftsmen have laid down is sound, because sometimes it is necessary to see that a word is given the same meaning throughout an entire section. At the end of the section reference is made to "three months from the date of any such application," and in another case reference is

Customs Act

to the appeal. I mention that as a matter of the use of words and not because it is very important.

In view of the fact that, barring unforeseen contingencies, the present minister will probably have the administration of this act, I cannot let him go on with any assumption that merely ascertaining cost of production in this country as against price quoted by a foreign country can determine the question which the tariff board must determine in any one of its appeals. I should dislike to find my hon. friend preaching such a heresy to the Liberal doctrines as enunciated by his party. Let me give him a concrete example. It is very easy to determine cost of production in this country, but it has developed in cases already before the tariff board that the cost of production in Canada in some particular industry may be unduly high because of inefficiency of production, because of obsolete machinery, because of inadequate methods of operation. How can the tariff board determine what is the cost of production in this country-let me say, efficient cost of production-except by ascertaining-
That is the sense of the statute.

As a matter of fact that is the provision of the statute, if my recollection is correct. How can the tariff board determine that question without ascertaining what is the cost of production in other countries, the methods, the wage scale, the machinery used and so on? I say to my hon. friend, from actual experience before the tariff board, that I know the board cannot determine some of the questions that must of necessity arise in appeals such as those contemplated here without ascertaining the cost of production in other countries, the efficiency of production, and so on. This tariff board, in my experience, has functioned particularly efficiently and I can assure my hon. friend that industries in Canada would have an easy time before the board in resisting applications for reductions in the tariff and in urging their own applications for increases if all they had to do was to prove cost of production under their method in Canada as against quotations from foreign competitors. I suggest to the minister that that factor as well as those suggested by the leader of the opposition and by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George should be seriously considered before he asks this committee to adopt the section in its present form.

The minister dealt with the question of price and cost. Those are not

National Harbours Board

That subsection (1) of section 3 be amended by striking out all the words after the word "minister" in line 22 on page 1 down to the end of the said subsection, and substituting therefor the following:-

Speaking to the point of order may I say that there must be some understanding about money bills. When a bill providing for the expenditure of money is submitted to parliament it must have the consent of the representative of his majesty. In turn the representative in Canada, as does his majesty in England, gives a blank cheque to the government. In such bills on most occasions there are no definite specifications with respect to expenditures. For instance, if the salary of the commissioners and members of the board are mentioned in the bill there must be additional expenditures for the stag. Very seldom in a money bill do we find anything definite regarding amounts of expenditures. For instance, when the bill was submitted to set up the employment commission no definite salaries were mentioned, although there was a provision for expenditure of money. On that occasion His Excellency the Governor General gave a blank cheque to the government for expenditures.
Further, we are in committee, and I suggest that when an hon. member moves an amendment accepted by the committee, the government must stand behind it, even if the ministers have to make an effort to swallow it. When the government introduces legislation providing for the expenditure of money it is the privilege of any hon. member in committee to suggest any changes he may wish, and it is up to the committee to decide whether or not the change shall be accepted. May I point out that what has been said so far is strictly in order. Further, it is the privilege of any hon. member to suggest a curtailment in expenditures. Any hon. member may move an amendment to decrease an expenditure, in which event the yeas and nays are taken and the majority rules. If Such action can be taken to decrease an expenditure it may also be taken to increase it. I have listened to the observations of the Minister of National Defence and I say he has not shown that the amendment of the hon. member for Laurier would have the efiect of increasing an expenditure. He has said nothing to satisfy the minds of hon. members that the amendment would have the efiect of increasing expenditures. I submit,
therefore, that hon. members who have spoken against the amendment were not in order and were all wrong, and I suggest, further, that the amendment is strictly in order and should be accepted by the committee.

I have also intimated to the house the high esteem in which I hold the present Minister of Marine. But during the course of his brief remarks he made a statement to which I must take exception. I do not think it is fair to cast a reflection upon the harbour boards that have displayed considerable efficiency and public zeal over a period of twenty to twenty-five years by a statement such as this, "a shocking betrayal of public trust." That might refer to certain boards in certain localities, or to certain members of certain boards, but I do not think the Minister of Marine would care to make such a sweeping statement in connection with all harbour boards that have been in existence in connection with our national harbours or in respect of all members of those boards. In justice to these men who have so faithfully dis-

charged their duties and in justice to those boards that have displayed considerable efficiency I feel that the minister should, and I hope that he will, qualify his statement and qualify it considerably. I know there are harbour boards and certain individuals against whom we could level such accusations, and probably in some cases they would be well founded, but I must say this: I do know certain members of certain harbour boards; I am conversant with the administration given by certain harbour boards in certain of the larger cities of Canada, and I must say that the minister's statement cannot apply to certain harbour boards and to certain individuals who have served on those boards. I refer particularly, of course, to the harbour board that has just ceased to exist in Montreal. I refer particularly to the chairman of that harbour board. He is a man in whom I have the utmost confidence. There are others that I could name in other cities, and no doubt other hon. members are interested in harbour boards in their own particular cities and could cite numerous examples on whose behalf exception should be taken to the minister's statement. I would ask the minister if he would place on Hansard a qualification of his statement so that all harbour boards will not be included and so that all gentlemen who have served on harbour boards will not be included in such a sweeping and general statement.

To read certain documents he takes from certain papers with reference to harbour boards and members of harbour boards scattered all over this country from Halifax to Vancouver, men who have given their lives to the service of their country? Does he assail Professor Brock, whose life is gone? He assails him. He assails decent men in Montreal, Halifax, Saint John, men who have given their very best to their country. He now says that this is the most shameless breach of trust that has ever happened in the Dominion of Canada. He has said too much or too little, and if he makes that statement he cannot read from a document without these men having a chance to be heard and offering any explanation they desire. These men cannot be charged ex parte. There must be an opportunity afforded by a parliamentary committee for these men to appear and make their explanation. The minister says that his remark applies to no period and to no particular board. Therefore it is universal. It covers all the harbours we have in Canada. It covers their administration for years before he was in Canada. His statement refers to men who value their reputation just as much as he values his, men who are as honourable and have as decent a record as business men as he has, men whose reputation will stand the closest investigation that may be brought to bear upon it by any tribunal. These men have a right to be heard. I thought when the minister rose that I would hear a decent explanation with regard to his statement, but he not only repeats it but emphasizes it. Now it is quite clear that these men must have a chance to be heard. It is no good to say: I have here a lot of information. That is not under oath. What importance can one attach to that?
We have had cases of this kind before in this country and we know perfectly well that opportunity for defence must be given. During the last parliament charges were made with respect to the Montreal harbour. Charges were made in the press with respect to the guaranteeing of securities amounting to $19,000,000 for the building of a bridge in that harbour. One of the first things we did after coming into office was to appoint a firm of auditors, Price, Waterhouse and Company, to make an investigation. They did investigate and made a report which was tabled in this house and which contained a detailed history of the expenditures for the construction of that bridge. It was alleged by an hon. member who sat for a western constituency that there were improper things in connection with it, but we satisfied ourselves from facts that were produced to the auditors that we would have to go entirely beyond Canada in order to deal with what was alleged, and we had no jurisdiction.
In connection with the harbour at Halifax there was an investigation that was partly completed. This was carried on under Mr. Justice Orde, who has since died. I notice an item in the estimates providing for the payment of certain accounts which were incurred. These men and their successors are now suffering under that charge. The men at Saint John and their successors are in the same position, and the same applies to the men at Three Rivers, Chicoutimi and Quebec and their successors. Is that fair? I do not think there is any harm in saying to the minister that he is inexperienced. No minister would ever think of making a charge of that kind against men who cannot be heard, who are not here, who have not an opportunity to appear, who have wives and families, whose honour and good names are just^ as valuable as the hon. gentleman's Their children are proud of their fathers and no one has a right to make a charge of that kind without giving them a chance to be heard. There is only one way in which this matter can be dealt with; it should be referred to a proper committee for the purpose of investigating the charges which he makes against these men during the years they have administered these harbours as commissioners.

speechtext:
On the second reading of this bill I expressed my opinion as to the merits and demerits of the principle involved therein. I suggested then to the government that every section of the country should retain as much local autonomy as possible. Very little good can accrue to Canada from the centralization of the control of our harbours in the hands of three government officers sitting in Ottawa. No matter how
National Harbours Board

distinguished, how alert or how efficient they might be, these gentlemen could not accomplish as much as three local boards, one on the Pacific, one on the Atlantic and one on the St. Lawrence river. The minister suggested difficulties which might arise in the appointment of the commissioners. He suggested that in the maritime provinces a difficulty might arise as between Saint John and Halifax and on the St. Lawrence, between Quebec, Three Rivers, Montreal, Sorel and Chicoutimi. These difficulties, in my opinion, are insignificant as compared with the discontent which will certainly arise in these various cities over the loss of the autonomous government of their harbours
There is much colour and substance in the statement made by the minister as regards certain things needing correction. The harbour boards were not infallible and I am free to admit that mistakes were committed. As long as we shall have to rely upon human beings to administer our harbours, mistakes will be committed. The three men to be selected by the government, no matter how carefully selected, will not be infallible and they will make mistakes. But I submit that well selected men, conversant with local conditions, would be of greater service than three government officials sitting in Ottawa. No matter how devoted these men might be in the discharge of their duties, they could not possibly be as efficient as men chosen in the locality.
Progress reported.
